conventional_description: In Western medicine, thick yellow or green nasal discharge is typically a sign of sinusitis - inflammation of the sinus lining, often triggered by a viral or bacterial infection, allergies, or structural issues. The color change comes from immune cells fighting off the infection, and the thickness reflects increased mucus production and congestion. Diagnosis is usually based on symptoms, sometimes with a nasal endoscopy or CT scan if the condition becomes chronic. Treatment aims to reduce inflammation, clear the passages, and address any infection.
conventional_treatments: Standard care includes saline nasal rinses, decongestant sprays or pills, and intranasal corticosteroids to reduce swelling. If a bacterial infection is suspected, a course of antibiotics may be prescribed. For chronic or recurrent cases, doctors might recommend longer-term steroid sprays, allergy management, or even surgery to open blocked sinus passages.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the nose is the outward opening of the Lungs - so when the Lungs are affected by a pathogen, the nose is often the first place it shows. Thick or yellow nasal discharge signals that Heat has entered the body, either from an external invasion like a cold or flu, or from an internal imbalance that generates Heat and Dampness. The Lungs normally keep Qi descending and fluids moving smoothly, but Heat disrupts that function, cooking normal mucus into a thicker, yellower form and pushing it upward into the sinuses.
But the Lungs are only part of the story. The Stomach and Spleen manage the body's fluids - when a diet heavy in greasy, sweet, or rich foods overwhelms them, they produce Dampness and Heat that can rise into the sinuses just like steam from a boiling pot. The Gallbladder, closely tied to the Liver, can also send Heat surging upward when emotional stress and frustration build up. In each case, the discharge is thick and yellow, but the pattern behind it - and therefore the treatment - is completely different.
This is why TCM doesn't treat all sinus discharge the same way. A sudden yellow discharge with a sore throat and mild fever points to Wind-Heat invading the Lungs and needs a different herbal strategy than a chronic, foul-smelling discharge with irritability and a bitter taste, which signals Gallbladder Heat. TCM looks at the whole picture - the texture, smell, accompanying symptoms, tongue, and pulse - to identify not just that there is Heat, but where it's coming from and how to clear it at the root.

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner begins by asking about the color, smell, and texture of the discharge, plus what else the person feels. These details help separate patterns that all produce thick or yellow mucus but arise from very different root imbalances.
When the mucus appears early in a cold, is yellow and not especially foul, with a mild fever or sore throat, the picture points toward Wind-Heat invading the Lungs. The tongue tip is often red, and the pulse feels floating and rapid, confirming an acute external attack that needs to be released.
If the discharge is copious, thick, sticky, and yellow, and the person describes a heavy, blocked sensation in the nose along with poor appetite or a bloated feeling, Damp-Heat in the Stomach is likely. The tongue coating is yellow and greasy, and the pulse is slippery and rapid, reflecting internal turbidity rising upward.
When the mucus turns yellow-green and has a noticeable foul odor, and the person feels irritable, with a bitter taste in the mouth or one-sided headache, Gallbladder Heat is the usual culprit. The tongue body is red with a yellow coating, and the pulse is wiry and rapid, signaling heat transmitted from the Liver-Gallbladder axis.
Phlegm-Heat in the Lungs produces thick, yellow mucus that is hard to expel, often with a sensation of chest oppression or a productive cough. The tongue appears red with a yellow greasy coating, and the pulse is slippery and rapid, indicating that heat and phlegm are lodged deeper in the respiratory system rather than just the nasal passages.
Toxic-Heat is suspected when the discharge becomes purulent, possibly blood-streaked, and is accompanied by intense local pain, swelling, and systemic signs like high fever. The tongue is deep red with a dry yellow coating, and the pulse is rapid and forceful, reflecting a more severe infection that demands urgent clearing of heat toxins.

patterns.why_this_happens: Wind-Heat is an external pathogen that enters through the nose and mouth, attacking the Lung system first. The Lungs normally keep Qi descending and diffusing, but when Heat lodges there, it disrupts this flow and pushes turbid fluids upward into the sinus passages. This results in thick, yellow nasal discharge, congestion, and the accompanying throat and respiratory symptoms.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red tip with a thin yellow coating. Pulse: floating and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Heat is an exterior pathogen that attacks the Lung system; rest and warm fluids support the body's defensive Qi to push it out. Spicy and fried foods add internal Heat, worsening the discharge and throat symptoms. Wind exposure further drives the pathogen deeper, while steam inhalation helps open the nasal passages and moisten the mucosa.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Drink plenty of warm water and herbal teas like chrysanthemum or mint. Use a humidifier or steam inhalation to soothe nasal passages. Avoid spicy, fried, and greasy foods that generate internal Heat. Rest well and stay out of wind and drafts.

patterns.symptoms: ["Thick, yellow, sticky nasal discharge, often foul-smelling", "Feeling of heaviness in the head and body", "Upper belly fullness, nausea, and poor appetite", "Sticky taste in the mouth, bad breath, thirst with little desire to drink"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, fried, or heavy meals, Dairy products and sugar, Alcohol and spicy foods, Overeating or eating late at night, Damp, humid weather, Sedentary lifestyle
patterns.better_with: Light, bland diet (congee, steamed greens), Eating small, regular meals, Avoiding dairy, sugar, and greasy foods, Gentle movement after eating, Warm, dry environment
patterns.why_this_happens: The Stomach and Spleen are responsible for transforming food into clear Qi and sending turbid waste downward. When a diet rich in greasy, sweet, or heavy foods combines with a hot, damp constitution, Damp-Heat accumulates in the middle burner. Instead of descending, this turbid heat rises along the Stomach channel-which connects to the nose-and spills into the sinus passages, producing a thick, yellow, sticky discharge. The Dampness makes the mucus heavy and difficult to clear, while the Heat gives it a yellow color and a foul odor.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a thick, yellow, greasy coating; there may be red prickles in the centre. Pulse: slippery (Hua) and rapid (Shu), especially prominent at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat in the Stomach is directly fueled by diet. Greasy, sweet, and dairy foods generate Dampness, while alcohol and spicy foods add Heat. Overeating overwhelms the Stomach's ability to descend turbidity, forcing it upward into the nose. A light, bland diet removes the raw materials for Damp-Heat. Gentle movement and a dry environment help the Spleen transform and transport fluids, preventing stagnation. By cutting off the source of turbid heat, the nasal discharge naturally clears.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, sweet, and dairy-heavy foods that create Dampness, as well as alcohol and spicy foods that add Heat. Eat light, easily digestible meals such as congee, steamed vegetables, and small portions of lean protein. Chew thoroughly and avoid overeating. Gentle movement after meals, like a short walk, supports the Spleen in transforming Dampness. Keep your living environment dry and well-ventilated.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the body fails to transform fluids properly - often due to a rich diet or a lingering illness - Phlegm builds up in the Lungs. If Heat then combines with this Phlegm, it becomes thick, yellow, and sticky. Because the Lungs open into the nose, the turbid Phlegm-Heat rises and obstructs the nasal passages, producing a dense, yellow discharge that is hard to blow out.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly swollen at the front, with a yellow greasy coating and sometimes red prickles on the front third. Pulse: slippery and rapid (滑数 huá shuò), strongest at the right cun (Lung) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy and spicy foods create more Phlegm and Heat, directly adding to the pattern, while damp weather worsens the internal Dampness that feeds Phlegm. Overexertion and alcohol weaken the Lungs and stir up Heat. Cool, dry air and light meals reduce the burden on the Lungs and help clear the sticky obstruction. Steam inhalation moistens and loosens the thick mucus so it can drain, and sitting upright uses gravity to assist the Lung Qi in descending.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid dairy, greasy, and spicy foods - they generate Phlegm and Heat. Choose light, easily digestible meals with cooling vegetables like radish and pear. Steam inhalation with eucalyptus or peppermint can help loosen thick mucus. Gentle daily movement such as walking supports the downward flow of Lung Qi.

faqs.question: What does thick yellow nasal discharge mean in Chinese medicine?
faqs.answer: It means there is Heat - and usually Dampness - affecting your sinuses. The color and thickness tell us that normal fluids have been overheated and turned into turbid, sticky mucus. But the real question is where that Heat is coming from: your Lungs (from a cold or flu), your digestion (from rich foods), or your Liver and Gallbladder (from stress and frustration). Each source needs a different treatment.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help clear my sinuses?
faqs.answer: Yes - acupuncture can be very effective for sinus congestion and discharge. Points like Yingxiang LI-20, right beside the nose, and Hegu LI-4 on the hand help open the nasal passages, reduce inflammation, and guide Heat out of the body. Many patients notice they can breathe more easily during or right after a session, and regular treatments help correct the deeper pattern so the problem doesn't keep coming back.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results?
faqs.answer: For a recent, acute sinus issue, you might feel relief within a few days of herbs and one or two acupuncture sessions. Chronic or recurrent thick discharge usually takes longer - often 3 to 6 weeks of consistent treatment to see lasting change, because we're not just drying up the mucus but rebalancing the system that keeps producing it.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs with my antibiotics or steroid spray?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes - Chinese herbs can work alongside conventional medications, and many people use both while transitioning to a more root-focused approach. Always tell both your TCM practitioner and your doctor exactly what you're taking. There are no common dangerous interactions with standard sinus medications, but certain herbs that move Blood (like Dang Gui or Chuan Xiong) may need caution if you're on blood thinners.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet to get better?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a big role, especially if your pattern involves Dampness or Phlegm. In general, reducing dairy, sugar, greasy or fried foods, and alcohol makes a huge difference because these all create more Dampness and Heat in the body. Favor warm, light foods like congee, steamed vegetables, and ginger tea. Your practitioner will give you more specific guidance based on your exact pattern.

faqs.question: Will the thick discharge come back after TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: That's the goal - to stop the cycle. TCM doesn't just suppress the symptom; it strengthens your body's weak points, whether that's your Lung defenses, your digestion, or your ability to handle stress. When the underlying imbalance is corrected, many people find that sinus problems that used to come back every season or after every cold simply stop recurring.
